problem: The sentence 'R² = 0 means predicting ȳ' is a shorthand a student can read as an exact equivalence. R² = 0 really means the model's squared error equals that of always predicting the mean; the model itself need not output the constant ȳ.
fix: R² = 1 is perfect; R² = 0 means the model does no better than always predicting ȳ (it has the same squared error as that constant predictor); negative R² is worse than the mean.

problem: The axes are not named. 'Plots recall against 1−specificity' leaves students unsure which quantity goes on which axis, and the usual exam point (TPR on the vertical axis, FPR on the horizontal axis) is missing.
fix: ROC plots the true-positive rate (recall) on the vertical axis against the false-positive rate (1 − specificity) on the horizontal axis, as the threshold moves.

problem: Only 0.5 and 1.0 are described. A student may not know that an AUC below 0.5 means the scores rank the classes in the wrong order (worse than random), not just 'bad'.
fix: AUC 0.5 is random ranking, 1.0 is perfect ranking; below 0.5 means the ranking is inverted, i.e. worse than random.

problem: Telling students to 'report the mean and the standard deviation' without a caution invites them to treat this SD as the uncertainty of the mean CV score. The spread of k fold scores is not the standard error of the mean and is itself noisy when k is 5.
fix: Report the mean fold score and the SD across folds, but state that this SD is a rough spread, not the standard error of the mean CV score; small differences between models can be noise.

problem: The figure shows a single train/test pair, while five-fold CV repeats the split five times. The '5 scores' edge from one test box can mislead a reader into thinking one held-out fold produces all five scores.
fix: Add to the caption or a node note that the split rotates five times, each fold serving once as the test fold, and the five held-out scores are averaged.

problem: The answer says AUC 'does not reward a model that always predicts the majority class' without giving the value, so the student cannot see why. Such a constant-score model gets AUC 0.5.
fix: Add: a model that gives every case the same score (for example, always predicting the majority class) gets AUC 0.5, the random level, while its accuracy can look high on imbalanced data.
